newsitem.title: UK: Britain says Bosnia peace force likely to remain.
newsitem.headline: Britain says Bosnia peace force likely to remain.

text.p: British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind on Monday said it was likely there would be a NATO-led peacekeeping operation in Bosnia next year but said a fixed timetable for withdrawing troops should be agreed first. NATO's political wing on Monday reviewed what to do when the current force's mandate expires on December 20, and officials said no one had opposed the idea of keeping troops in Bosnia. "I believe it is likely that there will be a continuation force, that there will be seen to be a need for some ongoing international military presence," Rifkind told journalists.

"I believe that there should be a clear exit strategy in a finite period of time because we're now coming, I believe, towards the latter phase of the international military presence," he said. Rifkind said fewer foreign troops would be needed on the ground as local forces of law and order gradually gained strength and could command the confidence of the population.

"The follow-up force will still be significant but I hope we will see a phased reduction leading to a total military withdrawal," he said, adding that the current 60,000-strong Implementation Force (IFOR) had achieved many of its military aims.

NATO military chiefs want to see IFOR reduced by about half, with a substantial force based locally to prevent and deter any renewed conflict. Politicians want a similar reduction but with a rapid reaction force based outside Bosnia.

Rifkind was speaking during a briefing on a London conference which is due to be held on December 4 and 5 to discuss how to consolidate peace in Bosnia. He said the 50 foreign ministers expected to be at the talks alongside the international aid agencies needed to consider: * what practical steps could be taken to improve freedom of movement in Bosnia * how to help the country's new independent television network and establish a national telephone system * a definitive programme for the reform and restructuring of the Bosnian economy, including the establishment of a central bank and functioning ministries for economic management * how to help create police forces in Bosnia which could command goodwill and trust of the population * identifying which targets should be set for the return of refugees next year and what could be done to encourage them to return * how to persuade the various parties to live up to their commitments on cooperation with the international war crimes tribunal in the Hague * what goals should be required from the parties on the arms control commitments made in last year's U.S.-brokered Dayton agreement, which ended the war * whether the post of international mediator -- currently occupied by Carl Bildt -- should continue to exist next year and whether the mediator's authority and coordinating powers could be strengthened.
